summary: Draft cites 91 of 206 vault notes and covers all 13 decomposition sub-questions plus all required sections and formats. The gaps are clusters of evidence the corpus holds that would sharpen or qualify claims already in the draft. Three of them weaken the advocate-register steel-man or the provenance discipline: the 'audited absence' on decompilation ignores janus-llm in the vault; the pro-cross-vendor case omits the self-preference-bias evidence; and the P0 dependency auto-merge tier ignores direct evidence that agents choose vulnerable versions more often than humans. Length (78KB) is well above the 45-55KB norm.

findings.location: ## 3. Reverse Engineering & Codebase Mastery > 3.1, paragraph 'Decompilation is an audited absence'
findings.issue: The draft says decompilation is an 'audited absence' because 'No measured study of LLM-agent decompilation accuracy exists in the evidence base.' It never says what was searched. It also leaves out the one decompilation tool the vault holds: janus-llm (MITRE), which translates binaries into source by combining Ghidra decompilation with LLM reasoning, and chunks code across 100+ languages into a Chroma vector store for RAG ingestion. The absence claim is only true in the narrow sense that no accuracy *measurement* exists; a working tooling pattern does exist. As written, a reader would infer there is no decompilation pipeline to build on. The deep-inference directive requires audited absences to state their search scope.
findings.evidence: [[github-janus-llmjanus-llm-leveraging-llms-for-modernization-through-intelligent]]: 'can translate a binary file into a programming language using Ghidra decompilation combined with LLM reasoning'; 'chunks code across over 100 programming languages... stores chunks in a Chroma vector database'. The same MITRE group's evaluation, [[leveraging-llms-for-legacy-code-modernization-challenges-and-opportunities-for-l]], is already cited in 3.1. Related uncited notes: [[how-to-understand-a-legacy-codebase-using-ai-before-changing-it]], [[codeflow-map-codebase-architecture-and-neel-shah]].
findings.recommendation: In the 'Decompilation is an audited absence' paragraph, add one or two sentences: a Ghidra-plus-LLM pipeline exists as open source (janus-llm, from the same MITRE group whose accuracy findings are cited above), so the factory's decompilation spike starts from that tooling pattern. What is absent is any *measured accuracy* for agent decompilation. Rewrite the absence claim to state its scope, e.g. 'the corpus contains tooling but no accuracy benchmark for LLM-assisted decompilation'. Optionally add janus-llm/Ghidra to the Code intelligence row of the §9 tech-stack table.

findings.location: ## 1. Zero-Hallucination > 1.2 Steel-man and 1.3 rule 4 'Critics are assigned by measured strength, not by vendor'
findings.issue: The draft argues against the brief's fixed 'Claude generates, GPT critiques' pairing, but under-states the opposing case for cross-vendor critics. It omits the strongest mechanistic argument for a different-vendor critic: LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations, and that self-preference rises linearly with self-recognition ability. Under the advocate register, a weakly stated opposing case is a defect. This evidence also strengthens the draft's own rule 2 (the information restriction), since self-recognition is a channel that a same-model fresh-context reviewer keeps. The position-bias papers are also uncited, although only CodeJudgeBench is used to justify the order-swap.
findings.evidence: [[llm-evaluators-recognize-and-favor-their-own-generations]]: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama 2 'disproportionately favor summaries they themselves generated'; GPT-4 reaches 73.5% self-recognition out of the box; self-preference strength is 'linearly correlated' with self-recognition, shown causally through fine-tuning. Uncited related notes: [[judging-the-judges-a-systematic-study-of-position-bias-in-llm-as-a-judge-acl-ant]], [[judging-llm-as-a-judge]], [[length-controlled-alpacaeval]].
findings.recommendation: In 1.2, or as a sentence opening rule 4 in 1.3, state the pro-cross-vendor case at full strength: self-preference bias is real and causal, so same-model review carries a structural leniency risk. Then explain why the draft's design still holds: the bias was measured on summarization judgments, while the code results in 1.2 show cross-model review asymmetric and execution-grounded evidence dominant. The bias is the reason the critic must emit executable evidence rather than verdicts. Optionally cite the position-bias study next to CodeJudgeBench in 1.4 and length bias in 1.3 rule 5 ('Prompts stay terse').

findings.location: ## 3.2 sweep table row 'P0: reachability-confirmed dependency bump ... Auto-merge to staging' and ## 8.2 Phase 3 'P0 patches to staging'
findings.issue: The draft's earliest production-adjacent auto-merge class is the agent-authored dependency bump. The corpus holds a large empirical study showing agents perform worse than humans at exactly this task, and the draft never mentions it. Leaving it out makes the P0 tier look better supported than it is. The study's own recommended mitigation (PR-time vulnerability screening plus registry-aware guardrails) also maps directly onto the draft's verification plane.
findings.evidence: [[understanding-security-risks-of-ai-agents-dependency-updates]]: across 117,062 dependency changes in 2,807 repos, agents chose known-vulnerable versions in 2.46% of additions/updates against 1.64% for humans; 36.8% of agent cases needed a major-version upgrade to reach a patch, against 12.9% for humans; agent dependency work produced a net vulnerability *increase* of 98, while human work produced a net *reduction* of 1,316; agents also spread edits across many small PRs.
findings.recommendation: Add two sentences after the sweep table or under the P0 row. Cite the study, and require that P0 dependency bumps pass a registry-aware check (target version not in a known-vulnerable range, no major-version jump without escalation to P1) before the staging auto-merge. Note that agents' habit of fragmenting edits into many small PRs argues for batching dependency bumps before human sign-off, which fits the draft's existing 'batched named-human sign-off'.

findings.location: ## 5.1 'Event-driven triggers, treated as untrusted input', ## 2.2 (Skills as attack surface), and ## 9 tech stack row 'Tools and Skills: MCP behind a scoped gateway'
findings.issue: The draft treats triggers and Skills as attack surfaces, but leaves out a whole corpus cluster on agent-specific attack classes that its architecture is exposed to: adaptive prompt injection against coding agents, MCP server and protocol vulnerabilities, and memory/experience poisoning. The last one matters most to the draft's own design: the factory's 'compounding asset' loop (traces retrain the FSM, failures become evals, blocked merges feed future context) is exactly the 'poisoned experience retrieval' surface MemoryGraft attacks. 'MCP behind a scoped gateway' appears in §9 with no evidence or controls behind it.
findings.evidence: [[prompt-injection-attacks-on-agentic-coding]]: adaptive attacks exceed 85% success against state-of-the-art defenses; 73% of platforms fail at least one of four trust boundaries; 30+ CVEs; Claude Code Skills are 'Markdown-based with only partial sandboxing and no marketplace review'. [[mcp-servers-the-new-security-nightmare-equixly]]: 43% of assessed MCP servers had command injection, 30% unrestricted SSRF-style fetching. [[security-best-practices-model-context-protocol]]: token passthrough forbidden; confused-deputy and SSRF to 169.254.169.254; progressive least-privilege scopes. [[memorygraft-persistent-compromise-of-llm-agents]]: implanting malicious 'successful experiences' into long-term memory exploits agents' semantic-imitation heuristic. Also uncited: [[owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026-owasp-gen-ai-security-project]], [[echoleak-the-first-real-world-zero-click-prompt-injection-exploit-in-a]].
findings.recommendation: In 5.1, after 'Every trigger is attacker-controllable text', add one sentence with the adaptive-injection success rate, to show that quarantine-as-data is necessary and that prompt-level defenses alone are not enough. In 2.2 or the 9 tech-stack row, add the MCP gateway controls the spec mandates: no token passthrough, audience-bound tokens, SSRF egress blocks on metadata endpoints, least-privilege scopes. In 7 (the OBSV -> REG learning loop) or 10.3, add a qualifier: traces and evals feeding the FSM and memory are a poisoning surface, so only traces from runs that passed the verification plane and came from authenticated triggers are admitted to training.

findings.location: ## 5.2 'Director and 100+ Workers' (paragraph 'The Director is mostly a workflow engine') and ## 6.4 auto-kill
findings.issue: The query frames the factory as 'mimicking a 5,000-person software company where different AI agents act as specialized departments.' The draft mentions departments only as a column in the trigger table and never engages the corpus evidence on role-emulating software-team MAS (ChatDev, MetaGPT) or how they fail. MAST is the largest empirical failure study in the vault: 1,642 traces, failure rates of 41-86.7%, and a ChatDev case where a role agent violated its role spec by terminating without the CEO agent's consensus, fixed by giving termination authority to one role. That evidence directly supports the draft's 'Director is a workflow engine' and outcome-token designs, and it names termination failures (FM-1.5 unaware of termination, FM-3.1 premature termination) as top failure modes, which is the risk 6.4 addresses.
findings.evidence: [[why-do-multi-agent-llm-systems-fail]]: 7 SOTA open-source MAS fail 41%-86.7%; failure modes split into System Design (37.17%), Inter-Agent Misalignment (31.41%) and Task Verification (31.41%); ChatDev CPO disobeyed its role spec; moving termination authority to the CEO agent raised task success. [[large-language-model-based-multi-agents-a-survey-of-progress-and-challenges]]: ChatDev and MetaGPT emulate CTO/PM/Engineer roles in waterfall flows; MetaGPT uses a shared message pool. Also [[promas-proactive-error-forecasting-for-multi-agent-systems]] (trace-Markov failure forecasting, complementing the FSM brake).
findings.recommendation: In 5.2, add two or three sentences. Role-emulating 'department' MAS such as ChatDev and MetaGPT exist, but fail 41-87% of the time, with a third of failures due to inter-agent misalignment. That is the empirical case for departments being Skill and permission scopes under a deterministic Director, not peer agents negotiating with each other. Note also that MetaGPT's shared message pool is the same shared-channel pattern 5.3 warns about. In 6.4, cite MAST's termination failure modes as the measured reason termination authority sits in the external supervisor rather than with the agent.

findings.issue: Rule 2 rests the independence argument on cross-model review evidence. The corpus has a code-specific source that states the mechanism directly: LLM-generated tests and specs 'corroborate rather than catch' errors, and plurality voting amplifies correlated errors. It also offers an alternative arbiter, semantic triangulation. This would strengthen the draft's thesis and add a second evidence line.
findings.evidence: [[reducing-hallucinations-in-llm-generated-code]]: plurality voting fails because LLMs produce correlated errors; LLM-generated tests 'often corroborate rather than catch errors'; semantic triangulation improves correct-program selection by 16% over test-generation and metamorphic baselines across GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 and Gemini 2.5 Flash, and handles inexact multi-solution problems.
findings.recommendation: In rule 2, add one sentence citing the correlated-error finding as the code-level reason the Test Author must not see the implementation. Optionally add one clause to 1.4 (arbiter) noting semantic triangulation as a measured tiebreaker for problems with multiple valid solutions, where exact-match tests fail.

findings.issue: The proof-carrying-findings control is argued only from false negatives and authZ blindness. The corpus has a vivid false-positive case that shows the opposite failure of autonomous security agents: noise volume that destroys triage capacity.
findings.evidence: [[nobodys-in-the-cockpit-risks-of-autonomous-ai-security-testing]]: cURL shut down its bug bounty after 95% of submissions were invalid, about a fifth outright AI-generated noise; major bug bounty platforms report 60-80% invalid submissions. Related uncited notes: [[how-are-ai-agents-used-in-penetration-testing-synack]], [[exploitgym-can-ai-agents-turn-security]].
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to the 'Proof-carrying findings' bullet: unvalidated AI security findings have already overwhelmed human triage (cURL closed its bounty at 95% invalid), which is why a finding without reproduction and a negative control pages no one. Note this is vendor-sourced (Synack).

findings.location: ## 6.4 'Auto-killing idle agents: the outcome token', step 3 'Route by token'
findings.issue: The CLEAN path 'archives the run, releases the sandbox' but never revokes the Worker's identity and credentials. The corpus ranks improper offboarding of non-human identities as the #1 NHI risk and frames agent termination as a Leaver workflow. The draft's kill-switch revokes credentials only on anomaly, not on routine self-termination, so routine archival leaves orphaned agent identities, an identity-hygiene gap.
findings.evidence: [[leaver-for-ai-agents-you-fired-the-ai-did-it-actually-leave-opnova]]: 'Improper offboarding is the #1 non-human identity risk. Why AI agents keep their access after the project ends'. [[owasp-non-human-identities-top-10-owasp-foundation]] (NHI1 improper offboarding).
findings.recommendation: Extend step 3 by a clause: every terminal token (CLEAN, ISSUE_FOUND or INCOMPLETE) also revokes the Worker's short-lived credentials and IAM session at the proxy, per OWASP NHI1. Optionally add `iam.revoke(job.runner)` to the CLEAN branch of `supervisor_tick` in 10.1.

findings.location: Whole document (78KB); specifically the exec summary 'thesis against its two strongest objections' (lines 16-20), ## 5.3 opening, ## 8.4 second paragraph, and ## 10.3
findings.issue: Bloat check B1. At about 78KB the draft runs well above the 45-55KB range of top-scoring reports. The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident is argued four times: exec summary paragraph 5 (safeguards-disabled counterfactuals), 5.3 (1,200 agents, 70,000 messages, shared cache), 8.4 ('powerful, persistent, and collaborative enough...'), and implicitly in 10.3. The invariant 'agents act; gates they cannot control decide; named humans sign' is restated in the exec summary, the 7 closing paragraph, 10.1 lead-in, 10.2 and 10.3. 8.4 repeats Berkeley's 'certify agents' point and the capability/oversight tension already made in the exec summary. The four 'evidence does not support' items in the exec summary are each re-argued at full length in their own sections.
findings.recommendation: Cut about 10-15KB with no loss of evidence. (1) Shrink the exec summary's skeptical-objection paragraph to two sentences and point to 5.3, where the incident data lives. (2) Delete the 8.4 'opposite pressure' paragraph's re-quotation of OpenAI, keeping only the four 'developments that would justify widening autonomy' as a compact list. (3) Merge 10.2 and 10.3 into one short closing paragraph, since 10.2 repeats 1.2-1.3 and 10.3 restates the invariant. Drop the 7 post-diagram restatement of the trust rule, which the diagram caption already states. Use the freed space for the coverage additions above.
